title: Given an array of numbers, find all unique triplets that add up to zero. Each triplet must be unique, and the solution should avoid duplicates. (LeetCode: 3Sum)
shortTitle: Triplet Sum to Zero (3Sum with Two Pointers)

s1_definition.profdef: The triplet-sum-to-zero problem, known as 3Sum, asks for all unique sets of three elements whose sum is zero. The standard approach sorts the array, then fixes each element in turn and uses a two-pointer scan over the remaining right portion to find pairs that complete the triplet. Sorting enables both the two-pointer squeeze and straightforward duplicate skipping, giving an n-squared time solution.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh has a list of signed adjustments on an account, some credits (positive) and some debits (negative), and he needs to find every unique group of three adjustments that perfectly cancel out to zero rupees. He first sorts the adjustments. Then he fixes one adjustment at a time, and for each fixed one he asks Priya to find two others from the remaining list that together cancel it, using the two-pointer trick of starting wide and squeezing inward. He carefully skips repeats so he never reports the same cancelling trio twice.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort, fix one, then two-pointer the rest; skip duplicates at every level.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The triplet-sum-to-zero problem, known as 3Sum, asks for all unique sets of three elements whose sum is zero. The standard approach sorts the array, then fixes each element in turn and uses a two-pointer scan over the remaining right portion to find pairs that complete the triplet. Sorting enables both the two-pointer squeeze and straightforward duplicate skipping, giving an n-squared time solution.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh has a list of signed adjustments on an account, some credits (positive) and some debits (negative), and he needs to find every unique group of three adjustments that perfectly cancel out to zero rupees. He first sorts the adjustments. Then he fixes one adjustment at a time, and for each fixed one he asks Priya to find two others from the remaining list that together cancel it, using the two-pointer trick of starting wide and squeezing inward. He carefully skips repeats so he never reports the same cancelling trio twice.

**One line to remember:** Sort, fix one, then two-pointer the rest; skip duplicates at every level.

sections.s2_technical:
The brute-force approach tries every triple, which is cubic time. The efficient method first sorts the array. Sorting costs n-log-n but unlocks two big advantages: the two-pointer squeeze and easy duplicate handling.

We iterate an index `i` from the start. For each `i`, the value `arr[i]` is the fixed first element of the triplet, and we need two more elements to its right that sum to `-arr[i]`. We set `left = i + 1` and `right = end`, and we run the same two-pointer logic as the pair problem: if the three sum to zero we record the triplet, if the sum is less than zero we move `left` right to increase it, and if more than zero we move `right` left to decrease it.

Duplicate avoidance happens at two levels. At the outer level, if `arr[i]` equals `arr[i - 1]`, we skip this `i` because any triplet starting with that value was already found. At the inner level, after recording a triplet, we advance `left` past any repeated value and retreat `right` past any repeated value, so the same pair is not counted again.

A finance usage example: suppose signed adjustments sorted are `[-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]`. Fixing -4, we look for a pair summing to 4 in the rest; 2 and ... nothing fits cleanly here. Fixing -1, we look for a pair summing to 1, and left at -1, right at 2 gives -1 plus 2 equals 1, so the triplet is `[-1, -1, 2]`. We also find `[-1, 0, 1]`. The duplicate -1 at the outer level is skipped so we do not repeat the same triplets.

The senior-level nuance: there is an early exit optimization. Once `arr[i]` is greater than zero, no triplet starting at `i` can sum to zero because the array is sorted and everything after is at least as large, so we break. Also, this template extends directly to the general k-sum problem by recursively fixing elements and dropping to a two-pointer scan at the base case. The sorting approach is usually preferred over a hash-set approach because it handles duplicate triplets cleanly without needing to canonicalize and store each found triplet in a set.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a reconciliation process where an account accumulates signed adjustments throughout the day: credits are positive and debits are negative. The audit team needs to identify every unique group of three adjustments that exactly cancel to zero, because such trios often indicate a reversal pattern worth reviewing. Checking every possible triple on a long list is cubic and far too slow.

Problem 2 — The same adjustment amount can appear multiple times, and the audit report must list each cancelling trio only once, never with duplicates. The solution must therefore skip repeated values carefully at both the fixed-element level and the pair level.

The code defines a `ReversalFinder` class with a `findZeroSumTriplets` method that sorts the adjustments, fixes each element, uses a two-pointer scan, and skips duplicates. A runnable demo seeds a list of signed adjustments and logs every unique cancelling triplet.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the signed adjustments `[-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4]`.

Step 1: The finder sorts the array to `[-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]`. Sorting groups equal values together, which is what makes duplicate skipping easy.

Step 2: The outer index `i` starts at 0, fixing -4. The inner `left` starts at -1 and `right` at 2. The sums tried are -4 plus -1 plus 2 which is -3 (too small, move left), and so on; no pair completes -4 to zero, so this anchor finds nothing.

Step 3: `i` moves to index 1, fixing the first -1. `left` starts at index 2 (the second -1) and `right` at index 5 (value 2). The sum -1 plus -1 plus 2 is 0, so the triplet `[-1, -1, 2]` is recorded. The method then skips duplicate values and both pointers move inward.

Step 4: Still anchored at the first -1, `left` is now at 0 and `right` at 1. The sum -1 plus 0 plus 1 is 0, so the triplet `[-1, 0, 1]` is recorded. The pointers cross and the inner loop ends.

Step 5: `i` moves to index 2, which is another -1 equal to the previous anchor, so it is skipped to avoid duplicate triplets. Remaining anchors are positive-leaning and produce no new zero-sum triplet.

Final output:

```
Oct 27, 2026 6:05:00 PM com.bank.recon.ReversalFinderDemo main
INFO: Found 2 zero-sum triplet(s): [[-1, -1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]
INFO: Cancelling trio: [-1, -1, 2]
INFO: Cancelling trio: [-1, 0, 1]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4]
    │ sort → [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]
    ▼
  fix i=-4 → two-pointer rest → no triplet
  fix i=-1 (first) → left/right squeeze
    │ -1 + -1 + 2 = 0 → record [-1,-1,2]
    │ -1 +  0 + 1 = 0 → record [-1,0,1]
  fix i=-1 (dup) → SKIP (same anchor)
    ▼
  result = [[-1,-1,2], [-1,0,1]]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The triplet-sum-to-zero problem, often called 3Sum, asks me to find every unique group of three numbers that adds up to zero. The brute-force cubic approach checks every triple, but the efficient solution is to sort the array first and then reduce the problem to a repeated two-pointer scan, which brings it down to n-squared time.

After sorting, I iterate through the array and treat each element as the fixed first member of the triplet. For each fixed element I need two more elements to its right that together equal its negation, and I find them with the two-pointer squeeze: a left pointer just after the fixed element and a right pointer at the end, moving left inward when the sum is too small and right inward when the sum is too large. Sorting does double duty here, because it both enables the squeeze and lets me skip duplicates cleanly: at the outer level I skip a fixed element equal to the previous one, and after recording a triplet I advance past any repeated values on both pointers, so no triplet is ever reported twice.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in reconciliation. An account accumulated signed adjustments through the day, credits positive and debits negative, and the audit team wanted every unique group of three adjustments that exactly cancelled to zero, because such trios often signalled a reversal pattern worth reviewing. The lists could be long, so the cubic check was out, and the sorted two-pointer approach produced a clean, duplicate-free list of cancelling trios that fed straight into case management.

The senior-level point I add is the early exit and the generalization. Once the fixed element is greater than zero, no triplet starting there can sum to zero because everything after it in the sorted array is at least as large, so I break out immediately. And the same skeleton of sorting, fixing elements, and dropping to a two-pointer base case extends directly to the general k-sum problem by recursion. I prefer this sorted approach over a hash-set approach precisely because it handles duplicate triplets naturally without having to canonicalize and store every triplet I find.
